text.p: Police in Northern Ireland have uncovered plans by pro-British "loyalist" extremists to murder government officials in Belfast, The Times reported on Monday.
A major review of security had been ordered after the discovery that car movements by staff working at the heavily fortified Anglo-Irish Secretariat had been monitored, said the newspaper.

More than 20 senior British and Irish officials work at the secretariat under the auspices of the 1985 Anglo-Irish Accord, which gives Dublin a greater say in the affairs of British-ruled Northern Ireland.
The Times said the Ulster Defence Association, the Ulster Volunteer Force, the Redhand Commando or the newly formed dissident Loyalist Volunteer Force would have been behind the planned attacks.
Security sources said they could not confirm The Times' report.
Sectarian and political violence is on the increase in Northern Ireland but, despite a number of attacks, the pro-British loyalists' ceasefire is still officially in force.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA), which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, ended a 17-month truce in February 1996 and has since carried out a series of bombings and shootings against British targets.
